incidents.name: Na Lao irrigation weir
incidents.location_label: Santi Suk, Nan Province, Thailand
incidents.river_or_facility: Na Lao irrigation weir
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain and strong currents washed away one side of the Na Lao irrigation weir and damaged the adjacent road.
incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain across Nan Province on 19 August 2026 damaged irrigation and road infrastructure. Khaosod English, citing the Nan provincial public relations office, reported that strong currents washed away one side of the Na Lao irrigation weir in Santi Suk district and damaged the road beside it. The same storm cut the Phayaeng–Kiew Muang approach to the provincial capital, stranded people on a Muap-stream bridge at Ban Nam Song, and was reported with a Highway 1256 (Pua–Bo Kluea) bridge collapse. Nation Thailand separately described flash floods and washed-out bridges in Pua, including a bridge in the Fai Chao weir area — a different named structure. No source fetched reported deaths at the Na Lao weir itself.
incidents.status: One side of the weir washed out; adjacent road damaged. Provincial heavy-rain warning in effect through at least 21 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: unknown
incidents.notes: Minor weir washout, not a reservoir-dam collapse. Fai Chao weir/bridge damage in Pua is a related flood impact, not merged into this record.
incidents.breach_size: one side of the weir washed away
incidents.investigating_agency: Nan provincial public relations office report

incidents.name: Kangimi Dam
incidents.location_label: Igabi LGA, Kaduna State, Nigeria
incidents.river_or_facility: Kangimi Dam
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: NSEMA warned of reported structural distress and visible cracks, with no breach reported as of 19 August 2026.
incidents.what_happened: The Niger State Emergency Management Agency issued an urgent public warning on Tuesday 18 August 2026 over reported structural distress and visible cracks at Kangimi Dam in Igabi LGA, Kaduna State. NSEMA Director-General Abdullahi Baba Arah said August rains raised the need for immediate technical assessment and that a major failure could flood downstream communities in Kaduna, Niger State, the FCT and adjoining areas. NSEMA asked the federal government, Kaduna State, dam operators, NEMA, the hydrological and meteorological agencies and security services to verify crack severity, map downstream risk and activate early warning and evacuation planning. Residents were told to stay calm, avoid waterways in heavy rain and ignore unverified rumours. No source fetched for this dataset reported a breach or uncontrolled release.
incidents.status: No breach reported as of 19 August 2026. Neighbouring-state emergency agency alert only; independent confirmation of crack severity by Kaduna/NEMA/dam operator not found in the articles fetched.
incidents.notes: This is a watch, not a failure. NSEMA is the downstream state's EMA, not the dam owner or Kaduna regulator.
incidents.downstream_risk: NSEMA said a major failure could flood communities in Kaduna, Niger State, the FCT and adjoining areas
incidents.investigating_agency: Niger State Emergency Management Agency (alert; not the dam owner)

incidents.name: Tarlac River flood-control dike (San Isidro, Zone 1)
incidents.region: Barangay San Isidro, Tarlac City, Tarlac
incidents.location_label: Tarlac City, Tarlac, Philippines
incidents.river_or_facility: Tarlac River flood-control dike (DPWH Contract ID 25CJ0310)
incidents.cause_summary: About 50 metres of a newly built flood-control dike collapsed as monsoon rain swelled the Tarlac River.
incidents.what_happened: Local outlet Tarlakenyo reported that about 50 metres of a newly built Tarlac River flood-control dike in Zone 1, Barangay San Isidro, collapsed around 04:00 on 17 August 2026 as monsoon rain swelled the river. The project, 'Repair / Rehabilitation / Improvement of Flood Control Structures along Tarlac River Control' under the 2025 GAA (about PHP 45.43 million, contractor GJE Builders Corporation), had been recorded 100% complete on 6 February 2026. DPWH Tarlac 1st District Engineering Office personnel assessed the damage while barangay officials, city and provincial governments, PNP and the Philippine Army sandbagged the new dike's end and part of an older dike. Vice Mayor KT Angeles said the contractor should restore the structure; Mayor Susan Yap warned residents to stay away because the collapse could widen or water could rise. No casualty figure appeared in the article fetched.
incidents.status: Partial dike collapse under emergency sandbagging and DPWH assessment as of 17 August 2026. Situation described as still volatile that day.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: unknown
incidents.notes: Single local-newsroom source plus on-the-record mayor/vice-mayor and DPWH presence. Prefer a national Philippine wire or DPWH release when one appears. Not a reservoir dam.

incidents.name: Lake Wynonah Dam
incidents.region: South Manheim Township, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania
incidents.location_label: South Manheim Township, Pennsylvania, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Plum Creek / Lake Wynonah (175-acre reservoir)
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: PADEP cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway and inability to pass a major flood.
incidents.what_happened: In a 14 August 2026 letter to the Lake Wynonah Property Owners Association, Kirk Kreider, acting chief of PADEP's Division of Dam Safety, declared the 1971 earthen Lake Wynonah Dam 'unsafe' and requested an immediate voluntary full drawdown of the 175-acre reservoir at up to one foot per day, with a formal order threatened if the association does not comply. The letter cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway, inability to pass a major flood, and temporary bracing of the top walls after a spillway collapse at the community's Fawn Lake Dam. Kreider wrote that 'unsafe' does not mean imminent failure, but that deficiencies could result in failure with loss of life or substantial property damage if not corrected. The lake had already been drawn down 10–15 feet in autumn 2025 after new seepage and a boil were reported. PADEP also said the high-hazard owner lacked required financial assurance.
incidents.status: PADEP unsafe designation and requested full drawdown in effect as of 17 August 2026 reporting; draft consent order/agreement with a four-week response window. Not an imminent-failure declaration.
incidents.notes: 2025 seepage drawdown is background. No 2026 breach. Fawn Lake Dam spillway collapse date was not independently sourced for this file.
incidents.downstream_risk: high-hazard dam; PADEP said failure could cause loss of life or substantial property damage if not corrected
incidents.investigating_agency: PADEP Division of Dam Safety

incidents.name: Bowersock Dam
incidents.location_label: Lawrence, Kansas, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Kansas River (Kaw) / Bowersock Mills & Power Company
incidents.cause_summary: Owner said one of four inflatable rubber crest bladders was punctured by floating trees and debris and ripped from end to end; the concrete dam remained intact.
incidents.what_happened: The Lawrence Journal-World reported on 13 August 2026 that one of four inflatable rubber bladders on the crest of Bowersock Dam had been punctured by heavy floating debris and ripped from end to end. Co-owner Sarah Hill-Nelson said the No. 2 bladder failure left a gap that dropped the upstream millpond about six feet. The concrete dam was holding; there was no downstream flood wave. The city of Lawrence said the Kaw River Water Treatment Plant continued to operate, though low pond levels are less efficient for intake and filtration. The run-of-river dam supplies Kansas's only hydroelectric plant and maintains the pond for the city's water intake. Hill-Nelson said a replacement bladder would take about four months and cost upwards of $300,000, and that this was the first time a Lawrence bladder had been destroyed beyond repair (a 2021 seam tear had been stitched). Exact calendar day of the puncture was described only as recently before the Thursday 13 August article.
incidents.status: Concrete dam intact; No. 2 inflatable crest bladder destroyed; millpond about six feet below normal; water plant operating; repair approach undecided as of 13 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: No evacuation reported; KU rowing expected to be disrupted by low water
incidents.notes: Not a concrete-dam collapse. Incident date is the Journal-World report date; the owner said the puncture happened recently before that Thursday. Background dam dimensions (length ~655 ft, height ~17.08 ft, 423-acre impoundment) are from Wikipedia/LIHI, not from the 2026 incident article.
incidents.volume_released: millpond dropped about six feet; volume not stated
incidents.breach_size: No. 2 rubber crest bladder ripped end to end; concrete dam intact
incidents.downstream_risk: No downstream flooding reported; low water affects city intake efficiency and KU rowing
incidents.economic_damage: replacement bladder estimated upwards of $300,000 plus installation; full cost undecided

incidents.name: Dikwena Chrome Tailings Storage Facility (Samancor)
incidents.location_label: Brits, North West, South Africa
incidents.river_or_facility: Dikwena Chrome mine TSF, Compartment 1B (unnamed tributary polluted)
incidents.cause_summary: The northern wall of Compartment 1B collapsed; the cause is not officially determined, and commentary about rainfall or over-deposition is not an official finding.
incidents.what_happened: The northern wall of Compartment 1B at Samancor Chrome's Dikwena tailings storage facility near Brits collapsed at about 17:30 on 13 August 2026, releasing almost all tailings/slimes stored in that compartment. The Department of Water and Sanitation said a railway embankment and berms at the adjacent Eland Mine stopped the slurry from reaching the R566 provincial road; mine infrastructure, a railway line and Eskom powerlines were damaged and an unnamed tributary was polluted. DWS, the Limpopo-Olifants Catchment Management Agency and the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources assessed the site; DWS issued a verbal directive stopping tailings deposition in any of the mine's TSFs pending investigation. Water samples were taken; laboratory results were still pending as of the 17 August government statement. EWN reported no fatalities or injuries; cleanup of access routes and power infrastructure was under way by 18 August.
incidents.status: Government investigation ongoing; tailings deposition halted; cleanup and water-quality testing in progress as of 18 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: No residential evacuation reported; sludge blocked Eland Mine (Maroelabult) access and cut power in Brits, Hennops and surrounding areas

sources.label: SAnews / Department of Water and Sanitation

incidents.notes: Cause not officially determined. Satellite/expert commentary in Daily Maverick discusses possible delayed rainfall infiltration and over-deposition; that is not an official finding.

incidents.name: Beiru River and Jialu River levee breaches
incidents.region: Henan (Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan; Chuanhui District, Zhoukou)
incidents.location_label: Jiaxian County, Henan, China
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Changqiao Town, Jiaxian); Xinhua: Yuxi Village Beiru breach
incidents.river_or_facility: Beiru River; Jialu River (Shaying backwater)
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened levee breaches on the Beiru and Jialu rivers.
incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened a levee breach more than 40 metres wide on the Beiru River in Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan, on the night of Wednesday 12 August 2026; more than 2,000 people were relocated and Xinhua reported no casualties. That breach was sealed on Friday night 14 August after nearly two days of sandbagging, because heavy plant could not reach the narrow levee crown. A separate eastern-embankment breach on the Jialu River in Chuanhui District, Zhoukou, opened around 23:00 on Thursday 13 August, widening from about 30 metres to about 117 metres under Jialu inflows and Shaying River backwater. China Daily and People's Daily/Xinhua said the Jialu breach was sealed on Saturday night 15 August after more than 2,000 emergency personnel worked the site; crews continued raising, reinforcing and sealing seepage. A Level-IV national disaster-relief response was activated for Henan.
incidents.status: Both breaches reported sealed (Beiru 14 Aug; Jialu 15 Aug). Embankment raising, reinforcement and seepage control continuing at Jialu as of 15–16 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: More than 2,000 relocated from the Beiru breach; Jialu displacement not separately quantified in the English Xinhua/China Daily reports used
incidents.notes: Two distinct levee breaches grouped as one living-database item because they were the same Typhoon Dolphin flood episode. Zero deaths is the Beiru figure stated by Xinhua; no separate Jialu fatality figure was published in the reports fetched.
incidents.breach_size: Beiru more than 40 metres wide; Jialu widened from about 30 metres to about 117 metres
incidents.downstream_risk: more than 2,000 relocated from the Beiru breach

incidents.name: Olde Mill Golf Club Dam
incidents.location_label: Laurel Fork, Virginia, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Olde Mill Golf Resort lake / Stone Mountain Creek drainage toward Big Reed Island Creek
incidents.cause_summary: Intense rain was followed by failure of the primary spillway pipe; DCR said it had received none of the required owner documents since 2006 and the last emergency action plan expired in 2012.
incidents.what_happened: Intense rain on the night of 2 August 2026 flooded the Laurel Fork area of Carroll County. Virginia DCR Regional Engineer Steven Bricker observed on 4 August that the Olde Mill Golf Club lake (normal pool near 300 acre-feet) was almost completely drained after a partial breach. DCR's 5 August letter to owner Norris Mitchell / MG Golf Facilities LLC stated the primary spillway pipe failed, creating a scour hole around the riser and significant sediment loss; the dam has a preliminary high-hazard classification and may not impound water until corrective action. Downstream residents told Cardinal News at least 20 properties were damaged and estimated losses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars; they allege the dam intensified flooding. DCR said it had received none of the required owner documents since 2006 and the last emergency action plan expired in 2012. Owners were dewatering and beginning repairs as of mid-August; Carroll County said it issued no live alert because it learned of the flood after it ended.
incidents.status: Lake largely drained; DCR unsafe / non-imminent-danger notice in effect; dam not allowed to impound until corrective action; owner working on dewatering and spillway repair as of 18 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: At least 20 properties damaged (resident estimate reported by Cardinal News); no official evacuation figure
incidents.notes: Causal share of downstream flooding versus the rainstorm itself is disputed by residents and not adjudicated. NID inventory pages are background only and were not used for 2026 incident facts.
incidents.owner_operator: Norris Mitchell / MG Golf Facilities LLC
incidents.volume_released: lake almost completely drained after a partial breach
incidents.breach_size: primary spillway pipe failed, creating a scour hole around the riser
incidents.downstream_risk: Laurel Fork area; at least 20 properties damaged (resident estimate)
incidents.economic_damage: resident estimates in the hundreds of thousands of dollars

incidents.name: Bagré Dam
incidents.region: Centre-Est / Bagré (downstream White Volta / northern Ghana on alert)
incidents.location_label: Bagré, Centre-Est, Burkina Faso
incidents.river_or_facility: Bagré Dam on the Nakambé / White Volta system
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: Ghana authorities monitored a possible controlled spill if rainfall pushed the reservoir to a stated threshold.
incidents.what_happened: Ghana's Water Resources Commission said on 4–5 August 2026 that SONABEL, operator of Burkina Faso's Bagré Dam, might begin a controlled spill from 11 August if the reservoir reached a critical level (WRC cited 232.93 m / 62.77% full on 4 August). NADMO later said SONABEL deferred the 11 August spill because upstream rainfall was lower than expected; as of that day the level was 233.08 m, 1.92 m below a 234.15 m threshold cited by NADMO. A Citi Newsroom report of SONABEL's 15 August update put Bagré at 233.24 m (77.35% full), 1.76 m below the 235 m normal reservoir level, and said SONABEL may open spillway gates if the level reaches 234.75 m, with public notice before any release. This is a seasonal controlled-spill watch, not a structural failure. Northern Ghana communities along the White Volta remained on alert.
incidents.status: No spill started as of the 15 August 2026 SONABEL figures reported by Citi Newsroom. Reservoir below stated spill thresholds; Ghana NADMO/WRC still monitoring.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: NADMO placed White Volta basin communities on alert (68 communities cited in Northern Region coverage); no flood from a 2026 Bagré spill reported in sources fetched
incidents.notes: Not a dam failure. Spill-threshold figures differ slightly across WRC, NADMO and the 15 August SONABEL update; all agree the dam had not spilled as of those reports.
incidents.reservoir_capacity: 1,700 million m³ at normal operating level 235 m
incidents.downstream_risk: White Volta basin communities on alert (68 communities cited in Northern Region coverage); no 2026 spill reported
incidents.investigating_agency: Ghana Water Resources Commission / NADMO monitoring

incidents.name: Chattamakhana Dam
incidents.location_label: Balangir district, Odisha, India
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Balangir district; ~18 km downstream of Lower Suktel)
incidents.river_or_facility: Chattamakhana Dam (about 18 km downstream of Lower Suktel Dam per the MLA letter)
incidents.cause_summary: The newly built dam suffered cut-off-wall and downstream-embankment damage in early-August rains; the MLA’s letter said the sanctioned design had reduced waterway, gates and impervious floor.
incidents.what_happened: Newly built Chattamakhana Dam in Balangir district suffered damage in rains in early August 2026. Balangir MLA Kalikesh Narayan Singh Deo wrote to Chief Minister (and water-resources minister) Mohan Charan Majhi saying the cut-off wall was washed away and downstream embankments failed, and asking for a time-bound independent technical inquiry with the State Dam Safety Organisation and outside experts. He said the EPC project's sanctioned design reduced waterway from 256 m to 206 m, gates from 18 to 14 and impervious floor from 80 m to 50 m, while design discharge stayed 2,760 cumec, and he questioned whether that flood had been reassessed after Lower Suktel Dam. New Indian Express and OrissaPOST published the letter on 8–9 August. No source fetched described a full dam collapse or casualties.
incidents.status: Embankment/cut-off damage reported; independent inquiry requested as of 9 August 2026. Not reported as a collapse. Government inquiry outcome not found in sources fetched.
incidents.notes: Facts on damage and design changes come from the MLA's written representation as reported by newspapers, not from a published government inspection report. Not a collapse.

Eleven Media, citing the President's Office Information and Public Relations Bureau, said that by 5 August floodwater had entered five Laymyethna wards, major town roads and 106 villages across four townships, with more than 30,000 people affected in Laymyethna Township alone. AHA Centre Flash Update No. 1 of 19 August, citing DDM Myanmar as of 18 August 16:30 UTC+7, reported flooding of five urban wards, major roads and 150 surrounding villages, with 63,000 people affected and 15,000 displaced households in Ayeyarwady (Laymyethna, Hinthada, Yekyi, Kyangin), plus 1 death in that regional tally. DDM and partners were still repairing breached embankment sections with geo-bags, sandbags and other works; the government had provided about USD 85,200 in assistance. Heavy rain was forecast to persist through 23 August.
incidents.status: Breach repair and flood control still under way as of the 19 August 2026 AHA update; further heavy rain warned.

incidents.name: Swift Creek Upper Reservoir
incidents.region: Afton / Swift Creek Canyon, Lincoln County, Wyoming
incidents.location_label: Afton, Wyoming, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Swift Creek Upper Reservoir (Lower Valley Energy hydro)
incidents.cause_summary: The sluice gate failed, causing an uncontrolled release; a camera inspection found catastrophic gate failure, destroyed panels and a broken operating rod.
incidents.what_happened: Lower Valley Energy said the sluice gate at Swift Creek Upper Reservoir failed in the early morning of 13 July 2026, causing an uncontrolled release that substantially drained the reservoir and carried sediment, trees and debris downstream (including material from a 2023 upstream landslide). Town of Afton staff told SVI the town water supply was not affected. CEO Bear Prairie later said a camera inspection found catastrophic gate failure, destroyed panels, and a broken operating rod; debris then partly plugged the opening and flows stabilised at a low reservoir level. LVE said the dam itself remains safe and is monitored. Permanent gate replacement requires FERC, U.S. Forest Service and other approvals, with at least a 60-day FERC review after the repair plan is submitted. The public was told to stay out of the reservoir bed and canyon.
incidents.status: Reservoir largely drained and held at a low level; dam reported safe and monitored; sluice-gate replacement plan in regulatory review as of late-July 2026 LVE/SVI updates. No deaths reported.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: No evacuation reported; public exclusion of reservoir and Swift Creek canyon
incidents.notes: Operator URL slug is misspelled (faolure) on the live LVE page. Category is sluice-gate incident, not an embankment collapse.

incidents.name: Liulan (六蓝) Reservoir
incidents.region: Hengzhou, Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region
incidents.location_label: Hengzhou, Guangxi, China
incidents.river_or_facility: Liulan Reservoir (Xiaoyi Town / Liulan village); discharge toward Yunbiao River / Yujiang
incidents.cause_summary: Typhoon Maysak rain caused Liulan Reservoir to overtop and breach on 6 July 2026.
incidents.what_happened: Typhoon Maysak rain caused Liulan Reservoir in Hengzhou to overtop and breach on 6 July 2026. Nanning raised flood-control emergency response to Level I; CCTV video showed a large release through the dam breach. At a 9 July news conference, Nanning Vice-Mayor Ding Wei said the Liulan breach had caused 26 deaths (5 then unidentified) and 7 people missing, while Guangxi overall had 39 dead and 9 missing — figures that could overlap pending DNA identification. Deputy water-resources director Zhai Jianjia said Liulan water had fallen below dam-foundation rock, the breach and discharge had largely stabilised, and crest access was restored that morning for dredging. Nanning reported 64,500 people evacuated or resettled by 11:00 on 9 July (54,500 in Hengzhou; 9,321 in Binyang).
incidents.status: Breach and downstream discharge reported largely stable as of 9 July 2026; search, identification, resettlement and a later State Council investigation were reported in subsequent Chinese coverage.

incidents.notes: Official 26 deaths is the Liulan-attributed figure from the 9 July Nanning briefing; regional Guangxi total was 39 dead / 9 missing and may overlap. Nearby Yunbiao (breach) and Liuwang (overtopping) are separate records.

incidents.downstream_risk: 64,500 evacuated/resettled across Nanning as of 9 July (54,500 Hengzhou)

incidents.name: Dudhkumar river protection dyke (Muriarhat)
incidents.location_label: Nageshwari, Kurigram, Bangladesh
incidents.river_or_facility: Dudhkumar River protection dyke, Muriarhat / Adarshapara
incidents.cause_summary: Nearly 40 metres of river-protection dyke collapsed as the Dudhkumar ran 22 cm above its danger level, and floodwater entered villages through the gap.
incidents.what_happened: The Daily Star of 30 June 2026 reported that nearly 40 metres of Dudhkumar river-protection dyke collapsed late the previous night (29 June; a farmer quoted the paper said Monday night) at Muriarhat in Bamandanga union, Nageshwari, Kurigram, as the river ran 22 cm above its 29.60 m danger level at Pateshwari. BWDB executive engineer Rakibul Hasan said floodwater entered villages through the gap; the Bamandanga Union Parishad chairman said at least eight villages and about 5,000 families were stranded. A farmer said water entered around 250 households. BWDB prepared bamboo piling and sand-filled geobags. A 5 July Daily Star follow-up said water was receding and BWDB had started placing geobags on an unfinished 300-metre stretch of a 3,100-metre right-bank embankment delayed by land acquisition. No death toll for the dyke breach was given in those articles.

incidents.what_happened: At about 08:00 on 8 September 2008 the retaining wall of an unlicensed iron-ore waste reservoir at the Tashan mine in Xiangfen, Linfen, Shanxi, collapsed. A mudslide inundated Yunhe village and a crowded market. Official final count: 277 dead, 4 missing, 33 injured. About 268,000 m³ of sludge covered 30.2 ha, up to 6 m deep. 1,047 people were displaced. WISE: 190,000 m³, 277 killed, 33 injured. Governor Meng Xuenong resigned; 58 people including 34 former officials were later sentenced (2010).
incidents.status: Closed illegal facility; criminal sentences 2010.

incidents.name: Lake Delton dike / Highway A washout
incidents.location_label: Lake Delton, Wisconsin, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Lake Delton / Dell Creek / Wisconsin River
incidents.cause_summary: June 2008 Midwest floods: lake water overtopped County Highway A (part of the north dike), eroded a new 400-ft channel to the Wisconsin River, and emptied the lake. The 1927 dam itself was not the breach location.
incidents.what_happened: On the morning of 9 June 2008, after heavy rain, Lake Delton overtopped County Trunk Highway A on the north shore. Water cut a ~400-ft-wide channel down ~40 ft to the Wisconsin River about 800 ft away. The 267-acre lake emptied in about two hours. Three homes washed away and two more were destroyed when foundations were undermined. Wikipedia list: 0 fatalities. The lake was repaired and refilled by Memorial Day 2009. State cost cited at $3.6 million plus $2.5 million by the village.
incidents.status: Channel filled and dam upgraded; lake reopened 2009.

incidents.name: Ulley Reservoir dam (spillway scour)

incidents.what_happened: On 25 June 2007, during the June 2007 UK floods, collapse of a masonry spillway at the 1870s Ulley earth dam (about 12.6 m high) scoured a hole reported as about 20 m long by 6 m deep in the embankment toe. About 700 residents of Whiston, Treeton and Catcliffe were evacuated; the M1 was closed between junctions 32 and 36. Seventeen high-volume pumps removed about 4 million litres per hour. incidents.river_or_facility: Vässinkoski dam / Vässinjärvi reservoir, Oreälven
incidents.cause_summary: Extreme rainfall produced inflow about twice the original design flood; the dam did not fail.
incidents.what_happened: During the September 1985 flood, inflow to the much larger Vässinkoski reservoir upstream of Noppikoski peaked at about twice the original design flood. SMHI and Svenska kraftnät describe the situation as critical; a failure was only just prevented. A failure here would have been far worse than Noppikoski (reservoir about 70 times larger).
incidents.status: Dam held; treated as a near-catastrophe in official dam-safety history.

sources.label: Svenska kraftnät — Från Noppikoski till Slussen

incidents.notes: Official near-miss, not a breach. Lake/power station also spelled Vässinjärvi / Vässinkoski.
incidents.reservoir_capacity: About 70 times Noppikoski; lake area 7.53 km², regulated 408–424 m a.s.l.

incidents.name: Val di Stava tailings dams (Prestavel)
incidents.location_label: Tesero, Trentino, Italy
incidents.river_or_facility: Prestavel fluorite mine tailings / Stava / Avisio
incidents.cause_summary: The upper Prestavel tailings basin failed onto the lower basin; the record does not establish a specific engineering mechanism.
incidents.what_happened: At 12:22 on 19 July 1985 the upper Prestavel tailings basin failed onto the lower basin. About 180,000 m³ of tailings plus eroded material flowed 4.2 km at up to 90 km/h through Stava to the Avisio. Ten people were later convicted of culpable disaster and manslaughter. It is one of Italy’s worst industrial disasters and a global tailings benchmark.
incidents.status: historical / Fondazione Stava 1985 is the official memorial and documentation centre
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 3 hotels, 53 homes and 6 industrial buildings destroyed
incidents.notes: Official toll 268 after presumed-death rulings. A 269th missing-person listing was later removed.
incidents.volume_released: about 180,000 m³ of tailings plus eroded material
incidents.downstream_risk: Stava and Tesero; 3 hotels, 53 homes and 6 industrial buildings destroyed
incidents.investigating_agency: Italian courts (ten people later convicted)

incidents.cause_summary: WISE: dam-wall failure due to liquefaction during earthquake.
incidents.what_happened: On 3 March 1985 Cerro Negro No. 4 copper tailings dam (Cia Minera Cerro Negro) failed by liquefaction in an earthquake. WISE: 500,000 m³; tailings flowed 8 km downstream. Deaths not given. Same earthquake also failed Veta de Agua No. 1.

incidents.name: Kvistforsen mirror dam 7 (1985 failure)
incidents.location_label: Skellefteå, Sweden
incidents.geo_source: sv.wikipedia.org Skellefteälven table — Kvistforsen power-station coordinates (mirror dam 7 is in the old river bed, not the main dam)
incidents.river_or_facility: Kvistforsen spegeldamm 7, old Skellefteälven river bed (mirror/cascade dams)
incidents.cause_summary: Spillway gate hoist failure during a high flood from the main Kvistforsen spillways caused overtopping and breach of the low cascade/mirror embankment.
incidents.what_happened: Ekström (ICSE6, 2012) documents complete failure of the lowest Kvistforsen mirror/cascade embankment dam when a spillway-gate hoist failed while the main station spillways upstream released an unexpectedly high flood. The dam was overtopped within about 15 minutes and eroded through at the left embankment/concrete transition. Rebuilt in 1986 with additional spillway gates in the breach.
incidents.status: Complete failure of the small mirror dam; reconstructed 1986.

sources.label: Ekström 2012 — Recent dam incidents and failures in Sweden (ICSE6)

incidents.notes: Peer-reviewed conference paper by Sweco dam engineer. Exact calendar date not extracted beyond year 1985. Current main-plant owner is Statkraft; 1985 owner not sourced. Separate from the May 2010 near-failure at the rebuilt dam.

incidents.name: Carsington Dam (construction slide)
incidents.location_label: Carsington Water dam, Derbyshire
incidents.river_or_facility: Carsington Dam / Carsington Water (Severn Trent)
incidents.cause_summary: Progressive shear through a yellow-clay core boot and thin in-situ yellow clay with solifluction shears left under the footprint.
incidents.what_happened: Still under construction and not impounding, Carsington's upstream face accelerated from 4–7 June 1984. A slide grew to about 1,625 ft of crest, with up to 43 ft lateral and 33 ft downward movement. Four workers had earlier been asphyxiated by CO2 from pyrite–limestone reactions in a drainage tunnel (ASDSO construction fatalities, not flood deaths). The failed fill was removed; a redesigned dam was finished 1991–92 and opened in 1992.
incidents.status: failed fill removed; replacement dam in service since 1992

sources.label: ASDSO Dam Failures — Carsington Dam (United Kingdom, 1984)

incidents.notes: 0 flood deaths. Four earlier construction asphyxiations noted by ASDSO.
incidents.investigating_agency: forensic investigation (Skempton, Vaughan, Rocke et al.)

incidents.name: Suorva eastern dam leakage / sinkhole
incidents.location_label: Jokkmokks, Sweden
incidents.river_or_facility: Suorvadammen (eastern dam), Akkajaure / Stora Lule älv
incidents.cause_summary: Leakage/internal erosion through or under the moraine core where rock and cement grouting under the core were not tight; that dam section was under full reservoir pressure for the first time since completion in 1972.
incidents.what_happened: On 4 October 1983 unusual turbid leakage was seen below the eastern dam; a crater/sinkhole was observed on the crest near the abutment. Leakage increased during the afternoon. Experts ordered an emergency drawdown of about 1 m on 5 October. After about a week the leak path was found and cement-grouted. Official investigation followed (report 1:1987). Academic sources report turbid leakage up to about 100 l/s, later reducing.
incidents.status: Incident contained by emergency drawdown and grouting; dam did not breach.

sources.label: SOU 1987:64 (official investigation of Suorva leakage Oct 1983)

incidents.notes: Cited in government bill as an example of a serious incident at a large dam. Height 67 m and 6 000 million m³ refer to the western/highest dam and full Akkajaure volume (Wikipedia). Leakage was in the eastern dam. A student PDF and academic papers give the 4 Oct 1983 timeline and ~100 l/s figure.
incidents.investigating_agency: Official investigation (report 1:1987 / SOU 1987:64)

incidents.name: DMAD Dam (Delta-Melville-Abraham-Deseret)
incidents.location_label: Sevier River about 5 miles northeast of Delta, Utah
incidents.geo_source: named Delta, Utah town centroid; dam was about 5 miles NE of Delta on the Sevier
incidents.river_or_facility: DMAD Dam, Sevier River
incidents.cause_summary: USACE had warned the spillway was undersized. After months of record 1983 snowmelt runoff the emergency spillway failed, releasing the reservoir. Gunnison Bend Dam 7-8 miles downstream was then deliberately breached with explosives to limit overtopping.
incidents.what_happened: On 23 June 1983 the emergency spillway of the 34-foot DMAD irrigation dam failed after four months of record Sevier River runoff, releasing about 17,000 acre-feet. The surge wrecked road, railroad and irrigation crossings, flooded Hinckley, Oasis, Sherwood Shores and Deseret, and forced about 1,000 people to higher ground. A transient later drowned trying to cross the flooded river on a wire (body never found).
incidents.status: historical failure; Gunnison Bend proactively breached the same day
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 1,000 residents evacuated (UPI 24 June 1983)

sources.label: UPI — Dam collapses in central Utah (24 June 1983)
Deseret News — Dams in Distress (24 April 1988)
The DMAD Dam Spillway Failure — The Engineering Issues (PDF)

incidents.notes: Death: unnamed transient; police assumed drowning, body never recovered (Deseret News / Utah SHMP).
incidents.investigating_agency: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers had previously rated the dam unsafe (1977-81 inventory)

incidents.name: Glen Canyon Dam tunnel spillways
incidents.location_label: Colorado River at Glen Canyon Dam / Lake Powell, Page, Arizona
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Glen Canyon Dam location (Page, Arizona / Colorado River)
incidents.river_or_facility: Glen Canyon Dam spillways, Colorado River / Lake Powell
incidents.cause_summary: First sustained use of the 41-foot tunnel spillways in June 1983 produced cavitation (initiated at calcite deposits on the invert at the elbow). Holes were gouged through concrete into Navajo sandstone. The dam itself did not fail.
incidents.what_happened: During the 1983 Colorado River flood, Lake Powell filled for the first time. Operators opened the left spillway on 2 June. On the morning of 6 June they heard rumbling and saw debris ejected; inspection found cavitation damage at the tunnel elbow. Both spillways were later run (left to about 32,000 cfs). Lake Powell peaked at 3,708.34 feet on 14 July. Post-event inspection found a hole in the left tunnel about 35 feet deep, 134 feet long and up to 50 feet wide. Air slots were added in the repairs.
incidents.status: repaired with aeration slots; dam remains in service

sources.label: USBR — Operation of Glen Canyon Dam Spillways, Summer 1983 (PAP-0714)

incidents.notes: Not a dam breach. Wikipedia describes fear that cavitation could connect to the reservoir and compromise the foundation; that did not occur.
incidents.investigating_agency: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation

incidents.name: Sipalay (Marinduque Mining) tailings dam
incidents.location_label: Sipalay, Negros Occidental, Philippines
incidents.river_or_facility: Sipalay copper mine tailings dam
incidents.cause_summary: WISE: dam failure due to slippage of foundations on clayey soils.
incidents.what_happened: On 8 November 1982 a copper-mine tailings dam operated by Marinduque Mining and Industrial Corp. at Sipalay, Negros Occidental, failed. WISE records a release of about 28 million tonnes and widespread inundation of agricultural land up to 1.5 m high. Wikipedia's largest-failures table gives a similar 30 million m³ / 28 million tonne scale. No fatality figure is given in those sources.
incidents.status: Historic tailings-dam failure; the Sipalay/Maricalum mine later closed.

sources.label: WISE Uranium — Chronology of major tailings dam failures

incidents.notes: Release reported as 28 million tonnes (WISE). Deaths not stated.

incidents.name: Tous Dam
incidents.location_label: Tous, Valencia, Spain
incidents.river_or_facility: Júcar (Xúquer) River
incidents.cause_summary: Extreme rain overtopped Tous Dam after spillway gates could not be operated because power and access failed.
incidents.what_happened: Extreme rain on 20 October 1982 overtopped Tous Dam after spillway gates could not be operated (power and access failed). The central embankment eroded after 19:00, producing a peak breach flow far above design. About 100,000 people were evacuated. Spanish courts later held that the eight deaths and damages were avoidable and that the State was civilly responsible.
incidents.status: historical / dam later rebuilt; landmark Spanish liability case
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 100,000 evacuated; ~200,000 affected
incidents.notes: Judicial/official dam-failure deaths are 8. Some regional accounts of the broader 1982 flood cite ~30 deaths.
incidents.reservoir_capacity: 52 million m³ at normal operation; 122 million m³ at crest
incidents.breach_size: central embankment eroded after 19:00
incidents.downstream_risk: about 100,000 evacuated; ~200,000 affected
incidents.investigating_agency: Spanish courts (State held civilly responsible)

incidents.name: Lawn Lake Dam (and Cascade Lake Dam)
incidents.location_label: Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Roaring River / Fall River / Estes Park
incidents.cause_summary: Lawn Lake failed by piping, releasing a flood that then overtopped and failed Cascade Dam downstream.
incidents.what_happened: The 1903 earthfill Lawn Lake irrigation dam failed by piping about 05:30–06:00 on 15 July 1982, releasing 674 acre-feet down the Roaring River. The flood killed one backcountry camper, then overtopped and failed Cascade Dam, killing two more campers at Aspenglen. Estes Park’s business district flooded before Olympus Dam stored the wave. USGS modelled the cascade; damages were about $31 million.
incidents.status: historical / Lawn Lake and Cascade not restored as dams; other aging park dams later removed
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 177 Estes Park businesses damaged; presidential disaster declaration
incidents.notes: Three deaths, all inside Rocky Mountain National Park.
incidents.owner_operator: Farmers Irrigation Ditch and Reservoir Company
incidents.downstream_risk: Roaring River, Cascade Dam, Estes Park business district
incidents.investigating_agency: USGS; Colorado State Engineer

incidents.name: Tyrone mine tailings dam
incidents.location_label: Tyrone mine, Grant County, New Mexico, United States
incidents.geo_source: Western Mining History mine record (Tyrone Mine, Grant County)
incidents.river_or_facility: Tyrone copper mine tailings dam
incidents.cause_summary: WISE, citing USCOLD/UNEP compilations: dam-wall breach after a rapid increase in wall height produced high internal pore pressure.
incidents.what_happened: On 13 October 1980 the Phelps Dodge copper-mine tailings dam at Tyrone, New Mexico, breached. WISE Uranium records a release of about 2 million m³, with tailings flowing about 8 km downstream and inundating farmland. Wikipedia's list of tailings dam failures repeats the same volume and runout. No fatality figure is given in those sources.
incidents.status: Historic tailings-dam breach; mine later continued under successor owners.

sources.label: WISE Uranium — Chronology of major tailings dam failures

incidents.notes: Fatality count not stated; deaths left null (unknown), not 0.

incidents.name: Machchhu-2 Dam (Morbi)
incidents.location_label: Morbi, Gujarat, India
incidents.river_or_facility: Machchhu River
incidents.cause_summary: The earthfill dam failed after rainfall produced inflows far above design (about 16,307 m³/s), and hundreds of metres of both embankments collapsed.
incidents.what_happened: The earthfill Machchhu-2 Dam failed on 11 August 1979 after rainfall produced inflows far above design (about 16,307 m³/s). Hundreds of metres of both embankments collapsed, sending a 12–30 ft flood into Morbi about 5 km downstream within 20 minutes. A Gujarat High Court record of 1981 cites official estimates of more than 1,800 dead and about ₹100 crore property damage. Independent estimates are much higher.
incidents.status: historical / among the deadliest dam failures; dam later reconstructed
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Morbi industrial town and Rajkot-district villages inundated
incidents.notes: Official/court figure at least 1,800. Unofficial estimates range to 5,000–25,000; mass graves hindered counting. Guinness once listed it as the worst dam burst before Banqiao figures were declassified.
incidents.breach_size: hundreds of metres of both embankments collapsed
incidents.downstream_risk: Morbi industrial town about 5 km downstream and Rajkot-district villages
incidents.economic_damage: about ₹100 crore property damage (Gujarat High Court 1981 record)
incidents.investigating_agency: Gujarat Commission of Inquiry; Gujarat High Court record of 1981

incidents.name: Church Rock uranium mill tailings dam
incidents.location_label: Church Rock, New Mexico, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: United Nuclear Church Rock mill / Puerco River
incidents.cause_summary: NRC and company consultants attributed the tailings-dam breach to differential settlement on collapsible soils.
incidents.what_happened: A crack in the United Nuclear Corporation tailings dam near Church Rock opened into a breach about 05:30 on 16 July 1979, releasing about 93–95 million gallons of acidic radioactive tailings solution and 1,100 tons of solids into Pipeline Arroyo and the Puerco River. The spill crossed onto the Navajo Nation. NRC and company consultants attributed failure to differential settlement on collapsible soils. It remains the largest radioactive release in U.S. history.
incidents.status: historical / mill later Superfund; Navajo Nation settlement; groundwater contamination persists
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: downstream Navajo communities along the Puerco; livestock watering and domestic use disrupted
incidents.notes: No immediate deaths recorded. Public-health and environmental harm to Navajo communities is the main documented impact.
incidents.volume_released: about 93–95 million gallons of tailings solution and 1,100 tons of solids
incidents.breach_size: 20-foot breach in the south cell
incidents.downstream_risk: downstream Navajo communities along Pipeline Arroyo and the Puerco River
incidents.investigating_agency: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission; New Mexico Environmental Improvement Division

incidents.name: Storvatn / Tårnedammen (Sør-Varanger)
incidents.location_label: Tårnet), Norway
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Tårnedammen 69°39′36″N 30°28′42″E; lake also at Wikipedia Storvatnet 69°39′27″N 30°30′13″E
incidents.river_or_facility: Storvatnet (Fálleveaijávri) on Tårnelva; Tårnet kraftverk (A/S Sydvaranger)
incidents.cause_summary: Wikipedia Tårnedammen (citing Møller, Norske Dammer vol. 2): the needle dam (nålestengsel of 4x4-inch planks) used for flood release could not take ice pressure and failed, after which the whole dam failed.
incidents.what_happened: The masonry dam at Storvatnet failed. Wikipedia Tårnet kraftverk: 3.8 million m3 released; 200 m of national road, a garage, two boathouses, the village prayer house and some cabins destroyed; rock entered the penstocks and Tårnet kraftverk (1.5 MW) was permanently closed. Tårnedammen article: ~5 million m3 emptied in two days; people were trapped in a house as water stood up the wall; no one injured. Lake fell 3–4 m below previous HRV.
incidents.status: failure; power plant abandoned; terrain below dam restored; lake now at a new natural level

incidents.name: Wadi Qattara Dam (main and secondary)
incidents.location_label: Wadi Al-Qattara, 33 km east of Benghazi, Libya
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Wadi Qattara Dam 32°01′36″N 20°24′18″E (main dam); secondary dam was 10 km downstream
incidents.river_or_facility: Wadi Qattara Dam (main and secondary)
incidents.cause_summary: A 1979 flood exceeded storage and discharge capacity, severely damaging the main clay-fill dam and destroying the secondary dam. A 1983 ASCE case study postulated cracking of a poorly compacted core and dispersive internal erosion under high gradients.
incidents.what_happened: A flood in 1979 severely damaged the main Wadi Qattara clay-fill dam (completed 1971, 55 m high) east of Benghazi and destroyed the secondary dam 10 km downstream. Wikipedia and FAO/engineering summaries report no fatalities. The main dam was later heightened 7 m and the secondary dam replaced with rock-fill in 2000-2004 (about US$30 million). Both original dams were designed by Coyne et Bellier.
incidents.status: main dam rehabilitated and heightened 2000-2004; secondary dam replaced; scheme operating
incidents.notes: Only the year 1979 is sourced. Wikipedia list reports 0 fatalities. Secondary dam coordinates 31.99528N 20.33444E.

incidents.name: Arcturus gold-mine tailings dam
incidents.location_label: Arcturus gold mine, Zimbabwe
incidents.river_or_facility: Corsyn Consolidated Mines Arcturus tailings dam
incidents.cause_summary: WISE: slurry overflow after continuous rain over several days.
incidents.what_happened: On 31 January 1978 the tailings dam at the Arcturus gold mine (Corsyn Consolidated Mines) overflowed after several days of rain. WISE: 30,000 tonnes released; 1 person killed; extensive siltation of a waterway and adjoining rough pasture.
incidents.status: Historic gold-tailings overflow.

incidents.name: Kodaganar Dam (Alagapuri Dam)
incidents.location_label: Kodaganar / Alagapuri Dam, Dindigul, Tamil Nadu
incidents.river_or_facility: Kodaganar Dam on the Kodaganar River (Cauvery tributary)
incidents.cause_summary: Gates could not be fully opened in a power cut; floodwater overtopped the earthen flanks and cut 20-200 m breaches.
incidents.what_happened: Kodaganar (Alagapuri) irrigation dam, built 1977 as an earthen/masonry structure 15.75 m high from foundation with five 3.05 m vertical-lift gates, failed after heavy rain in the Kodaikanal range. Staff only partly lifted the gates when power failed. Water overtopped the downstream slopes. Wikipedia's lead says collapse in 1977; the failure section and NPTEL place the flood in 1978. Many lives were lost downstream, especially in present-day Aravakurichi taluk; no official total is given. The dam was rebuilt and reopened in the mid-1990s at 12.75 m.
incidents.status: destroyed 1977/78; reconstructed and reopened mid-1990s
incidents.notes: Year conflict: Wikipedia lead 1977 vs body/NPTEL 1978. Incident date stored as 1978. Deaths 'many' — left null.
incidents.breach_size: breaches 20 m to 200 m along the embankment (Wikipedia/NPTEL)

incidents.name: Kelly Barnes Dam (Toccoa Falls)
incidents.location_label: Toccoa Falls, Georgia, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Toccoa Creek
incidents.cause_summary: After several days of heavy rain the dam failed; a federal board could not isolate a single cause, citing slope slide, piping, localized crest breach and embankment saturation.
incidents.what_happened: After several days of heavy rain, the earthfill Kelly Barnes Dam above Toccoa Falls College failed about 01:30 on 6 November 1977. The flood killed 39 people, many in a campus trailer park. A federal board (USGS, Corps, SCS, NWS) could not isolate a single cause, citing slope slide, piping, localized crest breach and embankment saturation. The dam was never rebuilt.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: campus and trailer park inundated; Toccoa water supply broken for days

incidents.name: Laurel Run Dam (No. 2)
incidents.region: West Taylor Township, Cambria County, Pennsylvania
incidents.location_label: Laurel Run Creek above Tanneryville, near Johnstown, Pennsylvania, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Laurel Run Dam (No. 2)
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain overtopped the earthen dam. Later commentary cited inadequate spillway design and ignored consultant warnings from the 1960s. Six other dams failed the same night; only Sandy Run also killed people (5).
incidents.what_happened: At 02:35 on 20 July 1977, during the Johnstown flood, Laurel Run Dam No. 2 failed, releasing 101 million US gallons down a 3-mile valley into Tanneryville. Forty people died, 9 homes were destroyed and 19 damaged. There was no warning system; most residents were asleep. Damage about $5.3 million. The dam was never rebuilt; the site is now Laurel Run Park.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Tanneryville: 9 homes destroyed, 19 damaged

incidents.investigating_agency: Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources; later civil suits (settled 1989)

Flood water entered the Conemaugh between St. Michael and South Fork at Ehrenfeld. Wikipedia and the ASDSO incident record attribute 5 deaths to this dam. incidents.location_label: Teton River, Idaho, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Teton River
incidents.cause_summary: The earthfill dam failed during first filling after seepage and piping through the abutment and core; reviews blamed design and foundation treatment on highly fractured volcanic rock.

Operators could not plug the leaks; the dam unzipped and released on the order of 240,000 acre-feet. Wilford, Sugar City, Rexburg and other Snake River Plain communities were flooded. incidents.name: Roppadammen / Roppdammen (Nordre Ropptjern)
incidents.region: Innlandet (then Oppland) / Gausdal kommune, Vestre Gausdal / Bødal
incidents.location_label: Gausdal, Norway
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Roppa kraftverk 61°14′25″N 10°03′30″E (power station; dam at Nordre Ropptjern)
incidents.river_or_facility: Roppa (tributary of Jøra / Gausa); Roppa kraftverk intake dam at Nordre Ropptjern
incidents.cause_summary: NTH professor Ragnar Heggstad: breach at the bottom outlet. First filling autumn 1975 was incomplete because of drought; an ice cap around the bottom outlet later melted and water entered the moraine fill. NVE Project Dam Safety later cites Roppa 1976 as a leakage/piping failure. Eyewitness saw a hole under the dam / an emergency gate in the basin rim wash out.
incidents.what_happened: The newly built intake embankment at Nordre Ropptjern failed on Constitution Day. About 3 million m3 of water, soil and rock ran down the Roppa in a couple of hours (peak ~800 m3/s). Farm Sagsveen was totally destroyed; Svea dwelling house was taken; 100 m of Rv 255 foundation and Forsetbrua on Jøra were damaged. No human deaths; livestock losses uncertain. Sheriff warned at 12:10 and rescued another elderly couple.
incidents.status: failure; dam rebuilt; power station commissioned 1977

sources.label: NRK — Norges verste dambrudd var da Roppadammen brast på en 17. mai
NVE climate/dam-safety article listing Roppa 17 May 1976 among last major Norwegian dam accidents

incidents.name: Fontenelle Dam
incidents.location_label: Green River, Fontenelle Dam, Wyoming, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Fontenelle Dam
incidents.cause_summary: During first filling, unprotected relief joints in the foundation cutoff allowed reservoir water to erode embankment soils (hydraulic piping) at the right/west abutment. Emergency rockfill and rapid drawdown prevented a full breach.
incidents.what_happened: On 3 September 1965 a leak at Fontenelle Dam's west abutment grew into a large downstream cavity (on the order of 80 ft wide, 50-60 ft deep, 170-200 ft long). About 10,000 cubic yards of embankment slid into the stilling basin. On 6 September a 15-by-20 ft sinkhole 30 ft deep opened on the crest, leaving only about 45 ft of dam between the hole and the downstream face. USBR dumped riprap and lowered the 345,000 acre-foot reservoir about 4 ft/day. Emergency releases flooded ranches and homes along the Green River. No deaths.
incidents.status: repaired 1965-68; still operating (USBR Seedskadee Project); later 1985 emergency drawdown and partial diaphragm wall

incidents.name: Swift and Two Medicine Dams (Blackfeet Flood)
incidents.location_label: Blackfeet Indian Reservation, Montana, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Birch Creek / Two Medicine Creek
incidents.cause_summary: A rain-on-snow storm produced extreme runoff; Swift Dam failed and additional Reservation deaths were attributed to extreme spillway discharge at Lower Two Medicine Dam.
incidents.what_happened: A rain-on-snow storm in early June 1964 produced extreme runoff across northwestern Montana. Swift Dam failed about 10:10 on 8 June, killing 19 people on the Blackfeet Reservation. Lower Two Medicine Dam also failed; nine additional Reservation deaths were attributed to extreme spillway discharge before that failure. USGS documented the flood; Gibson Dam overtopped but held.

Investigations linked the breach to foundation displacement along the Newport–Inglewood fault system, with oil-field operations later the subject of civil settlement.

incidents.location_label: Babi Yar clay-pulp dump above Kurenivka, Kyiv, Ukraine

incidents.river_or_facility: Kurenivka clay-slurry dam (Babi Yar / brick-factory impoundment)
incidents.cause_summary: A dam holding loam pulp from a brick factory above Babi Yar collapsed after rain. Wikipedia and later Ukrainian documentary work cite design flaws and poor maintenance.

incidents.name: Açude Orós (Presidente Juscelino Kubitschek de Oliveira)
incidents.location_label: Jaguaribe River at Orós, Ceará, Brazil
incidents.river_or_facility: Açude Orós on the Rio Jaguaribe
incidents.cause_summary: Partial collapse of the unfinished earth dam after torrential rain; DNOCS records water overtopping the wall under construction at 00:17 on 26 March 1960.

O Povo (2025 anniversary) says the right abutment gave way and reported 3.5 billion cubic metres released down the Jaguaribe, flooding Limoeiro do Norte, Jaguaribara, Jaguaribe and Aracati. incidents.cause_summary: A roughly 60 ft masonry dam built across the Balcones Fault Zone slid on its foundation after a flood put more than 11 ft of water over the crest. USGS contemporaneous report describes two about 250 ft sections shoved about 60 ft downstream without overturning.
incidents.what_happened: At 11:20 on 7 April 1900, after about 17 inches of rain in 48 hours and roughly 11 ft of overflow, a section of Austin's granite masonry dam about 300 ft from the east end gave way. Two sections each about 250 ft long slid 60-80 ft downstream. The current wrecked the powerhouse. USGS engineer Thomas U. Taylor recorded five employees and three boys drowned there. Lake McDonald emptied and Austin lost electric power for months. Later replaced by Tom Miller Dam in the 1940s.

incidents.name: Bouzey Dam (réservoir de Bouzey)
incidents.location_label: Avière valley at Bouzey, near Chaumousey / Épinal, Vosges, France
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Lac de Bouzey 48°09′52″N 6°21′22″E (rebuilt reservoir on the same site)
incidents.river_or_facility: Bouzey Dam (réservoir de Bouzey)
incidents.cause_summary: Masonry gravity dam on porous sandstone. A 1884 first-filling slide (about 35 cm downstream) left the profile cracked. On 27 April 1895 excessive uplift inside the masonry opened a roughly 170 m breach about 10 m below the water surface. Maurice Lévy's 1895 Académie des Sciences note made uplift a standard design load.
incidents.what_happened: The masonry Canal de l'Est feeder dam on the Avière failed suddenly around dawn, releasing nearly 7 million m3. The flood destroyed the hamlet of Bouzey and tore through Uxegney, Domèvre, Oncourt, Frizon and Nomexy before entering the Moselle. Engineering summaries and La Revue EIN give 87 dead. The dam had already suffered a major first-filling displacement in March 1884 and had been patched rather than rebuilt. It was reconstructed with a lowered water level in 1900-1901 and again in 1939.
incidents.status: rebuilt (1900-1901, 1939); present reservoir still feeds the Canal des Vosges
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Bouzey hamlet destroyed; Domèvre 28 houses and 32 dead; Nomexy 8 dead; railway and canal damaged

Commonly cited deaths exceed 100; some accounts put the toll as high as 150. The dam was never rebuilt.

incidents.what_happened: After a late spring of snowmelt and several days of heavy rain, the masonry/earth dam at Kobberdammen failed. The flood wave also destroyed Theisendammen and the dams below. Ten or more houses and mill buildings in Ila were destroyed.
incidents.status: historic_failure; dam later rebuilt (present masonry dam from 1908; rehabilitated 2003)

sources.label: NVE climate/dam-safety article naming 1791 as worst Norwegian dam accident
Trondheim kommune — Badevann og dammer (1791 and later Ilavassdraget failures)

incidents.notes: 18th-century event included because NVE treats it as Norway's worst dam disaster and the user asked for older named Norwegian failures. Cascade also took Theisendammen (not listed separately for 1791). Height/volume figures are for the present 1908 dam, not necessarily the 1791 structure.
incidents.owner_operator: Historically Ila mill owner (Thomas Jelstrup in 1791); present dam owned by Trondheim kommune
incidents.year_built: Dam on site since at least 1659; raised 1790; rebuilt after 1791; present form 1
incidents.reservoir_capacity: 0.25 mill. m3 (present NVE figure; 1791 volume not sourced)

incidents.name: Great Dam of Marib (final ancient breach)
incidents.location_label: ancient Marib dam on Wadi Adhanah / Dhana
incidents.river_or_facility: Great Dam of Marib (Sadd Marib / Dam of Arim)
incidents.cause_summary: Repeated breaches (recorded 449, 450, 542, 548) and rising siltation. Last repairs 557. Final overtopping about 570 or 575 left unrepaired. Quran 34:15-17 refers to the Flood of the Arim.
incidents.what_happened: The ancient packed-earth Marib dam, heightened over centuries to about 14 m under the Himyarites, finally failed about 570-575 CE and was not rebuilt. Wikipedia: the irrigation collapse is associated with migration of up to 50,000 people from Yemen. The English dam-failure list gives the date as 575 and cause as possibly neglect. A modern earth dam was built nearby in the 1980s (opened 20 December 1986).
incidents.status: ancient dam ruined; modern dam 3 km upstream opened 1986 (later war-damaged 2015)
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: migration of up to 50,000 people (Wikipedia)
